questions.question: Which of the following statements regarding metaplasia is true?

options.A: Metaplasia refers to the abnormal growth of cells, often leading to cancer.
options.B: It is a reversible change in which one adult cell type is replaced by another adult cell type.
options.C: Metaplasia is always a pathological process and never occurs in response to normal physiological stimuli.
options.D: Metaplasia is characterized by the replacement of differentiated cells with undifferentiated stem cells.

explanation.text: Metaplasia is a reversible process in which one adult cell type is replaced by another, typically in response to chronic irritation or inflammation. Either 1 epithelium can change into another or 1 mesenchymal cell can change into another mesenchymal cell In metaplasia, normal cells are involved.

**If cells are abnormal, then it is Dysplasia (Option A ruled out):** Metaplasia can sometimes occur in response to normal physiological stimuli (Option C ruled out) In metaplasis, the programming of stem cells is changing, because of which previous epithelium is replaced by new epithelium (Option D ruled out)

questions.question: Which of the following pathological conditions involves the accumulation of pigments through exogenous sources?

explanation.text: Among the given options, coal workers' pneumoconiosis involves the accumulation of pigments through exogenous sources. Pigments in pathology Endogenous pigments → produced inside the body (melanin, hemosiderin, bilirubin, lipofuscin). Exogenous pigments → come from outside (carbon, dust, tattoo ink). Pneumoconiosis Lung disease due to inhalation & deposition of exogenous dust particles.

Most common form → Coal workers’ pneumoconiosis (Anthracosis). Anthracosis (Black Lung Disease) Caused by the accumulation of carbon particles in alveolar macrophages (“dust cells”). Called Black Lung because the lungs appear black from heavy carbon deposition. The term Anthracosis comes from “Anthrakos” (Greek = coal/charcoal).

questions.question: A 83-year-old man presents to his gastroenterologist with complaints of fatigue and discomfort in the upper abdomen. He has a history of hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus, for which he takes medications regularly. On physical examination, the liver edge is palpable below the right costal margin, indicating hepatomegaly. Laboratory investigations reveal mildly elevated liver enzymes. Which of the following pigments is most likely responsible for the brown discolouration of the liver observed in this patient?

explanation.text: An 83-year-old man presents with fatigue and upper abdominal discomfort, and physical examination reveals hepatomegaly; mildly elevated liver enzymes are noted on lab tests, and the brown discoloration of the liver is most likely due to the pigment Lipofuscin. Lipofuscin, also known as lipochrome or wear-and-tear pigment, is an insoluble pigment derived from the peroxidation of polyunsaturated lipids in intracellular membranes.

It is a telltale sign of free radical injury and lipid peroxidation. It is responsible for the brown atrophy of the liver and heart, where lipofuscin accumulates in the hepatocytes and cardiac myocytes, respectively, due to oxidative damage and impaired cellular turnover, particularly with increasing age. It is also seen in senile atrophy (pigment of the old age).

In histopathological examination, it appears as a yellow-brown, finely granular cytoplasmic pigment, often deposited in the perinuclear region. The special stain used for lipofuscin is Oil red O and Acid-fast / Ziehl–Neelsen stain.

questions.question: A 45-year-old woman presents with a painless, slow-growing, pigmented lesion on her back with irregular borders and varying shades of brown and black. Excisional biopsy of the lesion is performed, and histopathological examination reveals nests of melanocytes within the dermis, with prominent melanin pigment deposition. Which of the following staining techniques would be most suitable for visualization of the melanin pigment within the melanocytes in this patient's biopsy specimen?

explanation.text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a painless, slow-growing pigmented lesion on her back characterized by irregular borders and varying shades of brown and black; histopathological examination of an excisional biopsy reveals nests of melanocytes in the dermis with prominent melanin deposition, best visualized using the Masson-Fontana stain.

Best for seeing the amount & distribution of melanin pigment (inside/outside melanocytes)-Masson–Fontana stain Other methods: Schmorl’s stain → also for melanin pigment. Enzymatic method (DOPA oxidase test) → best test for melanin production capacity.

Immunohistochemistry (for melanocytes / pigment-producing cells): HMB-45 Melan-A (Option D ruled out) It is a marker for melanocytes and melanoma cells and is particularly useful in distinguishing melanocytic lesions from other types of skin tumours or metastatic cancers.

On the other side, Masson Fontana staining helps to assess the extent of melanin production within tumors. (Option D ruled out) Key distinction: Pigment visualization → Masson–Fontana Cell identification (melanocytes) → HMB-45, Melan-A Masson Trichome stain (Option B): Masson Trichrome stain primarily differentiates between collagen and smooth muscle fibres.
**Periodic-Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain (Option C):** Periodic Acid-Schiff (PAS) stain detects carbohydrates such as glycogen and mucin.

questions.question: A 45-year-old man presents with complaints of fatigue, joint pain, and abdominal discomfort. On examination, he exhibits bronze-coloured skin pigmentation mainly on the face and hands. Laboratory tests reveal elevated serum ferritin levels and transferrin saturation. Which of the following staining techniques would be most appropriate to visualize hemosiderin deposition in tissues in this patient?

explanation.text: A 45-year-old man presents with fatigue, joint pain, and abdominal discomfort, along with bronze-colored skin pigmentation on the face and hands; laboratory tests show elevated serum ferritin and transferrin saturation, and the most appropriate staining technique to visualize tissue hemosiderin deposition in this patient is Perls' stain. Perl's stain, also known as Prussian Blue stain is the stain used to detect hemosiderin.

Gold standard for Fe³⁺ iron (gives blue color ). The given clinical scenario suggests the patient is suffering from Hemochromatosis, an iron overload disorder in which excessive iron is deposited in various tissues as hemosiderin, a golden yellow to brown, granular, or crystalline pigment.

**Lillie's stain (Option B):** Lillie's stain also known as Lillie-Mayer's hematoxylin-eosin stain might help in detecting Ferrous ions (Fe2+) but is not useful for hemosiderin, which is ferric iron (Fe3+) Rhodanine stain (Option C): Rhodanine is utilized as a selective stain for the detection and localization of copper ions that accumulate in tissues such as the liver and brain in copper metabolism disorders, such as Wilson's disease (not to be confused with Rhodamine in microbiology for Mycobacterium TB).

**Supravital stains (Option D):** Supravital stains are a group of dyes used to stain living cells or tissues without causing cell death. New methylene blue and Brilliant cresyl blue target ribonucleic acid residues in reticulocytes and provide the characteristic blue reticular staining pattern.

questions.question: Which of the following pathological conditions is associated with the 'Tabby cat' effect?

explanation.text: Diphtheria myocarditis is associated with the 'Tabby Cat' Effect. Fat accumulation in the heart gives a characteristic Tigroid or Tabby cat appearance, which appears as yellowish streaks (fatty change) alternating with reddish streaks (unaffected myocardium). This appearance is seen in conditions such as Diphtheria myocarditis Arrhythmogenic Right Ventricular Cardiomyopathy (ARVCM) Cell injury.
**Xanthomas (Option B):** Xanthomas are found in skin and in tendons.
**Cholesterolosis (Option C):** Cholesterolosis refers to the cholesterol-laden macrophages in the lamina propria of the gallbladder aka strawberry gallbladder.
**Fatty liver (Option D):** Fatty liver, also known as hepatic steatosis, is characterized by the abnormal accumulation of triglycerides within hepatocytes (liver cells).

questions.question: Which of the following stains is not typically employed for the detection of lipid accumulation in histological samples?

explanation.text: Toluidine Blue is not typically employed for the detection of lipid accumulation in histological samples. A special stain for Mast cells and Basophils. It is a metachromatic stain Solution - Blue coloured Colour stained to mast cells and basophils - Purple Stains for fat Oil Red O (Option C) Sudan Black B (Option A) Sudan IV (Option B) Osmium Tetroxide Note: Toluidine Blue is a special stain for Mast cells and Basophils.

questions.question: A 60-year-old woman presents with bone pain and tenderness over her lower back. Imaging reveals multiple lytic lesions in the vertebral column. Laboratory tests indicate anaemia, elevated serum calcium levels, and monoclonal gammopathy. A bone marrow biopsy confirms plasma cell proliferation. Microscopic examination of the biopsy reveals intracellular inclusions, as shown in the image. What is the composition of the intracellular inclusions marked in the image?

explanation.text: The clinical presentation is highly suggestive of multiple myeloma, a plasma cell dyscrasia characterized by bone pain, lytic lesions, anaemia, hypercalcemia, and monoclonal gammopathy. Microscopic examination of the bone marrow biopsy may reveal the presence of intracellular inclusions, such as Russell bodies (Immunoglobulins in the cytoplasm) and Dutcher bodies (containing Ig in the nucleus), within some plasma cells.

questions.question: Following the resection of the pituitary adenoma in a patient with Cushing's disease, which intracellular change is most likely in residual adenoma cells?

explanation.text: Following resection of a pituitary adenoma in a patient with Cushing's disease, the most likely intracellular change observed in the residual adenoma cells is Crooke's Hyaline Change. It is a histopathological finding seen in the pituitary gland, particularly in corticotroph adenomas associated with Cushing's disease.

In crooke hyaline change, the normal granular, basophilic cytoplasm of ACTH-producing cells becomes homogenous and paler due to the accumulation of intermediate cytokeratin (CK) filaments. These changes occur as a response to chronic hypercortisolism.

**Mallory-Denk bodies (Option A):** Mallory-Denk bodies or Mallory hyaline bodies are eosinophilic, intracytoplasmic inclusions composed of intermediate filaments, particularly cytokeratin 8 and 18, commonly seen in hepatocytes in conditions such as alcoholic liver disease.

**Lewy bodies (Option B):** Lewy bodies are eosinophilic intracytoplasmic inclusions composed of aggregated alpha-synuclein protein and are characteristic of neurodegenerative disorders such as Parkinson's disease and Lewy body dementia.
**Civatte bodies (Option D):** They are also known as Colloid Bodies/ Cytoid Bodies and are seen in Lichen Planus.

questions.question: Which of the following stains would be most appropriate for visualizing glycogen deposits?

explanation.text: Periodic acid-Schiff (PAS) stain would be most appropriate for visualizing glycogen deposits, among the given options.

**Glycogen is PAS +ve; Diastase sensitive Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) stain (Option A):** is a basic stain that stains nuclei blue-purple (hematoxylin) and cytoplasm and extracellular matrix pink (eosin). While it can highlight muscle fibre morphology, it does not specifically stain glycogen.

**Masson's trichrome stain (Option C):** is used to distinguish collagen fibers, which stain blue, from other tissue components; it stains muscle fibers red, collagen blue, and nuclei blue-black, but it is not specific for detecting glycogen Oil Red O stain (Option D) is used to detect lipids and fat droplets.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is incorrect about dystrophic calcification?

options.A: It occurs in damaged or necrotic tissues.
options.B: It is characterized by the deposition of calcium salts in normal tissues.
options.C: It is often seen in areas of chronic inflammation.

explanation.text: Calcium deposition is in dead or degenerating tissues. Dystrophic Calcification Metastatic Calcification Dead or degenerating tissues are seen. (Option A ruled out) There will be a normal blood calcium count. (Optin D ruled out) Some examples: Dead Parasite TB (chronic inflammation) (Option C ruled out) Atheroma Monckeberg Sclerosis It is also called calcific medial degeneration. It happens in the tunica media.

Calcium occurs blue in color It occurs only as an old age phenomenon without any clinical significance. Psammoma Bodies: It is present as a concentric lamellation. It shows an onion-peel appearance Seen in: Papillary carcinoma of thyroid. Papillary renal cell cancer. meningioma. Prolactinoma Serous Cystadenocarcinoma of ovary. Normal tissues are seen.

The blood calcium level is elevated The most common organ affected due to Metastatic calcification - The Lungs Some Examples: Hyperparathyroidism Cancer: RCC and Breast cancer show an increase of calcium. Vitamin D intoxication Milk alkali syndrome Multiple myeloma Sarcoidosis

questions.question: Which of the following case scenarios is not indicative of metastatic calcification?

options.A: A 60-year-old male with a history of chronic renal failure presented with shortness of breath and bilateral lung opacities on chest X-ray.
options.B: A 45-year-old female with spinal tuberculosis complained of back pain.
options.C: A 30-year-old male with a long-standing history of heavy milk and calcium carbonate intake now experiencing recurrent kidney stones.
options.D: A 55-year-old female with sarcoidosis demonstrated elevated levels of serum vitamin D and calcium.

explanation.text: In tuberculosis, tissue death and degeneration lead to dystrophic calcification, which occurs despite normal serum calcium levels. Tuberculosis can lead to dystrophic calcification in bone tissue, resulting in symptoms such as bone pain and fractures.

Metastatic calcification → elevated serum calcium Dystrophic calcification → normal serum calcium, dead/degenerating tissue There are four principal causes of hypercalcemia: Increased secretion of parathyroid hormone (PTH) with subsequent bone resorption, as in hyperparathyroidism due to parathyroid tumours, and ectopic secretion of PTH-related protein by malignant tumours Resorption of bone tissue, secondary to primary tumours of bone marrow (e.g., multiple myeloma, leukaemia) or diffuse skeletal metastasis (e.g., breast cancer), accelerated bone turnover (e.g., Paget disease), or immobilization.

Vitamin D–related disorders, including vitamin D intoxication, sarcoidosis (in which macrophages activate a vitamin D precursor), and idiopathic hypercalcemia of infancy (Williams syndrome), characterized by abnormal sensitivity to vitamin D (Option D ruled out) Renal failure, which causes phosphate retention, leads to secondary hyperparathyroidism. (Option A ruled out) A 30-year-old male with a long-standing history of heavy milk and calcium carbonate intake now experiencing recurrent kidney stones (Option C): This will lead to increased serum calcium levels whereas dystrophic calcification occurs despite normal calcium levels.

questions.question: Which staining technique is commonly used to visualize calcium deposits in tissues and is particularly useful for detecting minute amounts of calcium?

explanation.text: Alizarin Red S Stain is commonly used to visualize calcium deposits in tissues and is particularly useful for detecting minute amounts of calcium, giving red color to calcium deposits. Stains of Calcium: Von Kossa Stain Imparts black color to calcium. Alizarin Red S Imparts red color to calcium. Used for staining minor amounts of calcium. Calcein Fluorescent stain for calcium Azan Stain To differentiate mineralized bone from osteoid.
**Masson’s trichrome (Option A):** To differentiate collagen (blue) and muscle fibers (red).
**Prussian blue (Option B):** Used for staining Iron.
**Wright-Giemsa stain (Option D):** Used for hematology slides.

questions.question: Among the following, which molecule is required for the presentation of the antigens by the APCs to TH2 cells?

explanation.text: Antigen-presenting cells (APCs) such as dendritic cells, macrophages, and B cells play a crucial role in the adaptive immune response by presenting antigens to T-helper (TH2) cells. This process requires Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) Class II molecules, which are essential for the activation of CD4+ T cells, including TH2 cells. MHC Molecule Role: APCs process antigens and present them on their surface bound to MHC Class II molecules.

MHC Class II molecules interact with the T-cell receptor (TCR) on CD4+ T cells. This interaction is critical for the differentiation and activation of TH2 cells, which secrete cytokines to mediate humoral immunity.

Incorrect Options: NK cells (Option A) are part of the innate immune system and do not present antigens or directly interact with TH2 cells. G-protein coupled receptors (Option B) are involved in cell signalling but are not involved in antigen presentation to T cells. Lectin receptors (Option D) are involved in innate immune recognition, particularly of carbohydrate molecules, but they do not mediate antigen presentation to TH2 cells.

questions.question: Which of the following types of cell death involves activation of caspase enzymes?

explanation.text: Apoptosis and Pyroptosis involves activation of caspase enzymes. Apoptosis A tightly regulated suicide program where cells activate enzymes to degrade their DNA and proteins. It’s an active process eliminating irreparably damaged cells without causing inflammation or tissue damage. Driven by activation of caspases that cause DNA fragmentation Phases: (Option B) Initiation phase: Activation of caspases 8, 9, 10 triggers a cascade.

Execution phase: Terminal caspases 3, 6, 7 lead to cellular breakdown. Morphological features: Cell shrinkage Chromatin condensation Cytoplasmic blebs and formation of apoptotic bodies Phagocytosis of apoptotic bodies by macrophages Histopathology: Apoptotic cells appear as round/oval with intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm and dense nuclear chromatin fragments.

Pyroptosis It is a form of programmed cell death involving release of IL-1, a fever-inducing cytokine. Microbial products in cells activate the inflammasome complex. Inflammasome activates caspase-1, which converts inactive IL-1 to active IL-1. (Option B) Active IL-1 causes fever, inflammation, and leukocyte recruitment. Pyroptosis helps eliminate infected cells and triggers local inflammation.
**Necrosis (Option A):** is a form of accidental cell death that does not involve caspases.
**Necroptosis (Option C):** is a programmed form of necrosis that occurs independently of caspases.

questions.question: A diabetic male presented with seizures. Radiological examination shows a lesion. Histopathological examination shows liquefactive necrosis. What is the most important mechanism responsible for this?

explanation.text: Diabetic patient with seizures → raises suspicion for a brain lesion (possibly abscess, infarct, or infection-related pathology). Histopathology: liquefactive necrosis → classic type of necrosis seen in brain tissue. Liquefactive necrosis in brain is mainly due to hydrolytic enzyme action breaking down tissue. In the CNS, ischemia or infection activates microglia and infiltrating neutrophils. These cells release lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes.

Brain tissue is rich in lipids and has little structural stroma, so enzymatic digestion quickly converts tissue into a liquid mass. Mechanism: enzymatic degradation > structural breakdown → liquefactive necrosis.
**Mechanical (Option B):** Trauma can cause hemorrhage or contusion, but necrosis type is not primarily from mechanical injury alone, here histology points to enzymatic breakdown.

**Ischemic (Option C):** Ischemia in most organs causes coagulative necrosis, except in the brain, where it still leads to liquefactive necrosis, but the mechanism is enzymatic digestion, not ischemia per se.
**Pressure (Option D):** Increased intracranial pressure can cause herniation or atrophy, not liquefactive necrosis by itself.

questions.question: Which of the following is pro-apoptotic?

explanation.text: The correct answer is Bax, because it is a pro-apoptotic member of the Bcl-2 protein family. The Bcl-2 family regulates the intrinsic (mitochondrial) apoptosis pathway. Members are divided into: Anti-apoptotic: Bcl-2, Bcl-xL, Mcl-1 → preserve mitochondrial membrane integrity, prevent cytochrome c release.

Pro-apoptotic: Bax, Bak, Bok → promote mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilisation (MOMP), allowing cytochrome c release and caspase activation. Mnemonic: "Bax and Bak Break" (break the mitochondrial membrane) → pro-apoptotic. "Bcl and Bcl-xL Build" (preserve the membrane) → anti-apoptotic.

questions.question: Caspase-1 is primarily involved in which type of programmed cell death?

explanation.text: Caspase-1 plays a central role in Pyroptosis, a form of programmed cell death associated with inflammation. It is a form of apoptosis in which there is release of the fever-inducing cytokine IL-1. Microbial products entering infected cells are recognized by cytoplasmic receptors, activating the multiprotein complex inflammasome.

This complex activates caspase 1 which converts the inactive IL-1 to active IL-1, causing fever, inflammation and leucocyte recruitment. (Option B) Pyroptosis is the mechanism by which some microbes cause the death of infected cells and trigger local inflammation.

**Apoptosis (Option A):** is a controlled, non-inflammatory cell death involving caspases-8, -9, -3, and -7, but not caspase-1, and serves to remove damaged cells without triggering an immune response.
**Necroptosis (Option C):** is a programmed inflammatory cell death triggered when apoptosis is blocked, involving RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL—but not caspase-1, distinguishing it from pyroptosis.
**Necrosis (Option D):** is an uncontrolled, non-programmed cell death due to injury (e.g., trauma or ischemia), causing inflammation without involving caspases, including caspase-1.

questions.question: What is the mechanism for healing in the case of a 57-year-old male with a gradually developing swelling over the scalp region, pus discharge, and pain?

explanation.text: In this case, the mechanism for healing is granulation tissue formation. Granulation tissue is a type of connective tissue that forms during the healing process of a wound. It is composed of new blood vessels (angiogenesis), fibroblasts, and an extracellular matrix. Granulation tissue fills the wound defect and helps in the formation of new tissue. It appears as red, soft, and granular tissue on the wound surface.

Incorrect options: Option A: Granuloma formation: Granuloma formation is a type of chronic inflammation characterized by the aggregation of immune cells, typically macrophages, in response to persistent or resistant antigens. It is not the primary mechanism involved in the healing of the described wound.

Option B: Scab formation: Scab formation occurs during the initial stages of wound healing when blood components, such as fibrin and platelets, dry and form a protective crust over the wound. It is not the primary mechanism involved in the healing process after incision and drainage of an infected scalp swelling.

Option D: Neovascularization: Neovascularization refers to the formation of new blood vessels. It is an important step in wound healing, but in the context of the described case, granulation tissue formation is a more relevant mechanism for healing.

questions.question: The body of an 82-year-old man has been seen for a post-mortem to determine the cause of death. You are examining a histopathological slide containing a section of his cardiac tissue where you notice some pigmentation. Which is the substance that is seen in the image given below?

explanation.text: The histopathological image shows lipofuscin in the section of cardiac tissue. Lipofuscin is a yellow to red-brown pigment found in cardiac muscle cells, particularly around the nucleus in the hearts of elderly, debilitated people.
**Melanin (Option A):** is a black or brown pigment found in skin, hair, and certain brain areas, not typically seen in cardiac tissue.
**Hemosiderin (Option C):** is an iron-storage complex resulting from the breakdown of haemoglobin, typically associated with conditions like haemorrhage or hemochromatosis.

**Iron (Option D):** Elemental iron deposition in tissues is pathological and associated with diseases like hemochromatosis or chronic blood transfusions. Staining with Prussian blue would help confirm iron presence.
